title: Data Structures
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L core Data Structures curriculum covering arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hashing at a structural/operational level. Grounded against LASU's own CSC221 'Fundamentals of Data Structures' course description (elementary/structured data items, arrays, sparse matrices, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, hash coding, storage management). Kept distinct from CSC213 by focusing on structure definitions and operations rather than complexity analysis.

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of an array as a data structure?
options: Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations and accessed by index
Elements are linked via pointers and scattered in memory
It can only store elements of different data types
It automatically grows without any size limit
questions.correct_answer: Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations and accessed by index
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements in adjacent memory slots, which allows constant-time direct access to any element via its index.

questions.question: What is the main drawback of using a static array when the number of elements is not known in advance?
options: Its fixed size can lead to wasted memory or insufficient space
It cannot be accessed randomly
It cannot store integers
It requires a hash function
questions.correct_answer: Its fixed size can lead to wasted memory or insufficient space
questions.explanation: A static array has a fixed size determined at creation, so an inaccurate estimate leads to either wasted space or an inability to hold all required elements.

questions.question: What is a sparse matrix?
options: A matrix in which most of the elements are zero
A matrix with only one row
A matrix used exclusively for graph representation
A matrix where all elements are non-zero
questions.correct_answer: A matrix in which most of the elements are zero
questions.explanation: Sparse matrices contain a large proportion of zero-valued elements, so specialized storage schemes (like storing only non-zero entries) save memory compared to a full 2D array.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of a singly linked list node?
options: It contains data and a single pointer/reference to the next node
It contains data and pointers to both the next and previous nodes
It stores data in a fixed-size contiguous block
It cannot contain a null pointer
questions.correct_answer: It contains data and a single pointer/reference to the next node
questions.explanation: A singly linked list node holds a data field and one pointer referencing the following node in the sequence, with the last node's pointer set to null.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of a linked list over an array for insertions and deletions?
options: Insertions and deletions do not require shifting other elements in memory
Linked lists always use less memory than arrays
Linked lists support O(1) random access
Linked lists are always faster to traverse
questions.correct_answer: Insertions and deletions do not require shifting other elements in memory
questions.explanation: Because linked list nodes are connected via pointers rather than contiguous memory, inserting or deleting a node only requires updating a few pointers, not shifting other elements.

questions.question: What distinguishes a doubly linked list from a singly linked list?
options: Each node has pointers to both the next and previous nodes
It cannot be traversed backward
It has no head or tail
Each node stores two data values
questions.correct_answer: Each node has pointers to both the next and previous nodes
questions.explanation: A doubly linked list node maintains two pointers, enabling traversal in both forward and backward directions.

questions.question: In a circular linked list, what does the last node's pointer reference?
options: The first (head) node of the list
Null
Itself
The middle node
questions.correct_answer: The first (head) node of the list
questions.explanation: A circular linked list connects the last node back to the head node, forming a loop instead of terminating with a null pointer.

questions.question: Which principle governs how elements are added and removed from a stack?
options: Last-In-First-Out (LIFO)
First-In-First-Out (FIFO)
Random access
Priority-based ordering
questions.correct_answer: Last-In-First-Out (LIFO)
questions.explanation: A stack follows LIFO ordering: the most recently added element is the first one removed.

questions.question: What are the two primary operations of a stack?
options: Push and pop
Enqueue and dequeue
Insert and delete at head
Append and prepend
questions.correct_answer: Push and pop
questions.explanation: Push adds an element to the top of the stack, and pop removes the element currently at the top.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common real-world application of a stack data structure?
options: Managing function call returns (the call stack) and undo operations
Managing print job queues
Scheduling CPU processes in arrival order
Implementing a breadth-first search
questions.correct_answer: Managing function call returns (the call stack) and undo operations
questions.explanation: Program call stacks track function calls in LIFO order so that control returns to the most recent caller, and undo features similarly reverse the most recent action first.

questions.question: What happens when you attempt to push an element onto a stack that has reached its maximum capacity?
options: A stack overflow occurs
A stack underflow occurs
The oldest element is automatically removed
The stack resets to empty
questions.correct_answer: A stack overflow occurs
questions.explanation: Attempting to add an element to a full, fixed-capacity stack results in a stack overflow condition.

questions.question: Which principle governs how elements are added and removed from a queue?
options: First-In-First-Out (FIFO)
Last-In-First-Out (LIFO)
Random selection
Depth-based ordering
questions.correct_answer: First-In-First-Out (FIFO)
questions.explanation: A queue processes elements in the order they arrive: the first element added is the first one removed.

questions.question: What are the two primary operations of a queue?
options: Enqueue and dequeue
Push and pop
Peek and poke
Insert and rotate
questions.correct_answer: Enqueue and dequeue
questions.explanation: Enqueue adds an element to the rear of the queue, and dequeue removes the element from the front.

questions.question: What problem does a circular queue solve compared to a simple linear array-based queue?
options: It reuses freed space at the front of the array instead of wasting it after dequeues
It allows LIFO ordering instead of FIFO
It removes the need for a rear pointer
It eliminates the need for enqueue and dequeue operations
questions.correct_answer: It reuses freed space at the front of the array instead of wasting it after dequeues
questions.explanation: In a linear array queue, dequeued front space is wasted as the rear keeps advancing; a circular queue wraps the rear pointer back to index 0 to reuse that freed space.

questions.question: In a priority queue, how is the order of element removal determined?
options: By the priority assigned to each element, not the order of insertion
Strictly by insertion order (FIFO)
Strictly by reverse insertion order (LIFO)
Randomly
questions.correct_answer: By the priority assigned to each element, not the order of insertion
questions.explanation: A priority queue always removes the element with the highest (or lowest, depending on convention) priority first, regardless of when it was inserted.

questions.question: In tree terminology, what is the 'root' of a tree?
options: The single topmost node with no parent
Any node with no children
The deepest node in the tree
A node with exactly two children
questions.correct_answer: The single topmost node with no parent
questions.explanation: Every tree has exactly one root node, which is the topmost node and the starting point for traversals.

questions.question: What is a 'leaf' node in a tree?
options: A node with no children
The root node
A node with exactly one child
Any node at depth 1
questions.correct_answer: A node with no children
questions.explanation: Leaf nodes are the terminal nodes of a tree that have no descendants.

questions.question: What defines a binary tree?
options: Each node has at most two children, commonly referred to as left and right
Each node has exactly two children
Every node must have a parent
It contains only numeric data
questions.correct_answer: Each node has at most two children, commonly referred to as left and right
questions.explanation: A binary tree restricts each node to a maximum of two child nodes, though a node can have zero, one, or two children.

questions.question: What property must a Binary Search Tree (BST) satisfy?
options: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger
Every node must have exactly two children
All leaf nodes must be at the same depth
The tree must be perfectly balanced
questions.correct_answer: For every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger
questions.explanation: This ordering property is what makes a BST allow efficient searching: the left subtree contains only smaller values, and the right subtree only larger values.

questions.question: In an in-order traversal of a Binary Search Tree, in what order are the nodes visited?
options: Left subtree, then root, then right subtree
Root, then left subtree, then right subtree
Left subtree, then right subtree, then root
Right subtree, then root, then left subtree
questions.correct_answer: Left subtree, then root, then right subtree
questions.explanation: In-order traversal visits the left subtree first, then the current node, then the right subtree -- for a BST, this visits nodes in sorted ascending order.

questions.question: In a pre-order traversal of a binary tree, in what order are the nodes visited?
options: Root, then left subtree, then right subtree
Left subtree, then root, then right subtree
Left subtree, then right subtree, then root
Right subtree, then left subtree, then root
questions.correct_answer: Root, then left subtree, then right subtree
questions.explanation: Pre-order traversal visits the current (root) node first, followed by the left subtree, then the right subtree.

questions.question: In a post-order traversal of a binary tree, in what order are the nodes visited?
options: Left subtree, then right subtree, then root
Root, then left subtree, then right subtree
Left subtree, then root, then right subtree
Root only
questions.correct_answer: Left subtree, then right subtree, then root
questions.explanation: Post-order traversal visits both subtrees before visiting the root node itself, which is useful for tasks like deleting a tree or evaluating expression trees.

questions.question: What is a 'complete binary tree'?
options: A binary tree in which every level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right
A binary tree with exactly one node
A binary tree where every node has two children
A binary tree with no leaf nodes
questions.correct_answer: A binary tree in which every level is completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree fills all levels fully except possibly the last level, which must be filled left to right without gaps -- this property is essential for array-based heap implementations.

questions.question: What is a 'heap' data structure primarily used for?
options: Efficiently retrieving the minimum or maximum element (priority queues)
Storing key-value pairs for O(1) lookup
Representing hierarchical file systems only
Implementing FIFO queues
questions.correct_answer: Efficiently retrieving the minimum or maximum element (priority queues)
questions.explanation: A heap (min-heap or max-heap) maintains an ordering property that allows the minimum or maximum element to always be at the root, making it ideal for priority queue implementations.

questions.question: In a max-heap, what is true of the value at the root node relative to all other nodes?
options: It is greater than or equal to the values of its children
It is always the smallest value in the tree
It has no children
It is equal to the average of all node values
questions.correct_answer: It is greater than or equal to the values of its children
questions.explanation: The max-heap property requires every parent node's value to be greater than or equal to the values of its children, with the maximum overall value residing at the root.

questions.question: What is a graph, in the context of data structures?
options: A collection of vertices (nodes) connected by edges
A linear collection of elements accessed sequentially
A tree with exactly one root
An array of key-value pairs
questions.correct_answer: A collection of vertices (nodes) connected by edges
questions.explanation: A graph is a data structure consisting of a set of vertices and a set of edges connecting pairs of vertices, used to model relationships and networks.

questions.question: What is the difference between an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list for representing a graph?
options: An adjacency matrix uses a 2D array to indicate edges, while an adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbors
An adjacency list can only represent directed graphs
An adjacency matrix uses less memory for all graphs
An adjacency list cannot represent weighted edges
questions.correct_answer: An adjacency matrix uses a 2D array to indicate edges, while an adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list of its neighbors
questions.explanation: Adjacency matrices use a V x V array (efficient for dense graphs), while adjacency lists store each vertex's neighbors in a list (more memory-efficient for sparse graphs).

questions.question: What is a 'weighted graph'?
options: A graph in which each edge has an associated numeric value (cost/weight)
A graph with more vertices than edges
A graph that cannot contain cycles
A graph where all vertices have the same degree
questions.correct_answer: A graph in which each edge has an associated numeric value (cost/weight)
questions.explanation: In a weighted graph, edges carry numeric weights representing cost, distance, or capacity, which is essential for algorithms like shortest-path calculations.

questions.question: What data structure is typically used to implement the standard iterative Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal of a graph?
options: A stack
A queue
A hash table
A priority queue
questions.correct_answer: A stack
questions.explanation: Iterative DFS uses a stack (explicitly or via recursion's call stack) to remember which vertices to visit next, exploring as deep as possible before backtracking.

questions.question: What data structure is typically used to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS) traversal of a graph?
options: A queue
A stack
A binary search tree
A linked list only
questions.correct_answer: A queue
questions.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to visit vertices level by level, ensuring nodes closer to the starting vertex are explored before farther ones.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a hash function in a hash table (hash coding)?
options: To map a key to an index in the underlying array for storage and retrieval
To sort the elements of the table
To encrypt data for secure storage
To compress the size of stored data permanently
questions.correct_answer: To map a key to an index in the underlying array for storage and retrieval
questions.explanation: A hash function converts a key into an array index, allowing near-direct access for insertion, deletion, and lookup operations.

questions.question: What is 'open addressing' in the context of resolving hash table collisions?
options: Probing for the next available slot in the array itself when a collision occurs
Using a separate linked list for each bucket
Rejecting any key that causes a collision
Doubling the hash table size immediately on any collision
questions.correct_answer: Probing for the next available slot in the array itself when a collision occurs
questions.explanation: Open addressing resolves collisions by searching (probing) for another open slot within the same array, using strategies like linear or quadratic probing.

questions.question: What is 'garbage collection' in the context of dynamic data structures?
options: Automatic reclamation of memory that is no longer referenced or needed by the program
Manually deleting all elements from a data structure
Sorting elements by removing duplicates
A technique for balancing a binary tree
questions.correct_answer: Automatic reclamation of memory that is no longer referenced or needed by the program
questions.explanation: Garbage collection automatically frees memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable or in use, preventing memory leaks in languages that support it.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between static memory allocation and dynamic memory allocation?
options: Static allocation happens at compile time with a fixed size; dynamic allocation happens at run time and can vary
Static allocation is always slower than dynamic allocation
Dynamic allocation cannot be freed
Static allocation can only be used for arrays
questions.correct_answer: Static allocation happens at compile time with a fixed size; dynamic allocation happens at run time and can vary
questions.explanation: Static memory is allocated at compile time with a size fixed in advance, while dynamic memory (e.g., via malloc/new) is allocated at run time based on program needs.

questions.question: Which data structure would be most appropriate for implementing an 'undo' feature in a text editor?
options: A stack
A queue
A hash table
A graph
questions.correct_answer: A stack
questions.explanation: Undo operations reverse the most recently performed action first, which naturally matches the LIFO behavior of a stack.

questions.question: Which data structure would be most appropriate for managing print jobs sent to a shared printer in the order they were received?
options: A queue
A stack
A binary tree
A hash table
questions.correct_answer: A queue
questions.explanation: Print jobs are typically processed in the order they were submitted, which matches the FIFO behavior of a queue.

questions.question: What is 'Polish notation' (prefix notation), often discussed alongside stacks and expression trees?
options: A way of writing expressions where the operator precedes its operands
A notation where operators always come after operands
A binary encoding scheme for integers
A method for balancing binary trees
questions.correct_answer: A way of writing expressions where the operator precedes its operands
questions.explanation: Polish (prefix) notation places the operator before its operands (e.g., + A B instead of A + B), removing the need for parentheses and making it easy to evaluate with a stack.
